emergency.ateMacadamiaNuts.science.conte: Macadamia nuts contain an unidentified toxin that uniquely affects dogs' neuromuscular system. The compound causes reversible weakness and ataxia in hind limbs, likely through disruption of motor neuron signaling. Unlike many toxins, the exact mechanism remains unknown despite decades of clinical observation. Research by Morton (2002) established the LD50 at 2.4 g/kg. The toxin is heat-stable and present in all forms: raw, roasted, salted, and in baked goods. Symptoms are dose-dependent and typically resolve within 12-48 hours with supportive care (ASPCA, 2023).
Minimum toxic dose: 0.5 g/kg body weight (mild symptoms)
Source: Morton, 2002 — Journal of Veterinary Diagnostic Investigation
Example: A 15kg (33lb) dog eating 15g of macadamia nuts (approximately 12-15 nuts) would reach the minimum toxic threshold. A typical nut weighs about 1.2-1.5g.

emergency.ateMushrooms.science.content: Amatoxins (alpha-amanitin, beta-amanitin) are bicyclic octapeptides found in Amanita, Galerina, and Lepiota species. They inhibit RNA polymerase II, halting protein synthesis in hepatocytes. The liver is the primary target because amatoxins undergo enterohepatic recirculation. After ingestion, there is a 6-12 hour latent period, followed by a gastroenteritis phase, a brief false recovery (12-24 hours), then fulminant liver failure with coagulopathy, encephalopathy, and death. Treatment within 12 hours has a 90% survival rate; after 24 hours, survival drops to 30% (ASPCA, 2023).
emergency.ateMushrooms.toxicityData.exam: A single Amanita phalloides cap contains enough amatoxin to kill a 10-20kg dog. Partial ingestion is still life-threatening.

emergency.ateCookedBones.article.ogDescr: Emergency guide: Cooked bones can splinter and cause life-threatening intestinal damage.
emergency.ateCookedBones.banner.title: My Dog Ate Cooked Bones: What to Do Now
emergency.ateCookedBones.banner.subtitle: Cooked bones splinter into sharp fragments that can puncture the intestinal wall or cause life-threatening obstruction. This is a mechanical emergency, not a poisoning. Call your vet immediately.
emergency.ateCookedBones.science.content: Cooking denatures collagen in bones, making them brittle and prone to splintering. Raw bones contain flexible collagen and are less likely to fragment. When cooked bones splinter, sharp fragments (osteoids) can penetrate the GI wall, causing peritonitis — a life-threatening infection. The most common sites of perforation are the esophagus (if swallowed improperly), stomach, and ileocecal junction (where the small intestine narrows). Poultry bones are especially dangerous because they are hollow and shatter into needle-like shards (AAHA, 2023).
emergency.ateCookedBones.toxicityData.mi: N/A (mechanical hazard — any size fragment can cause damage)

emergency.ateCookedBones.toxicityData.ex: A single chicken bone can shatter into dozens of needle-like splinters that act like tiny knives in the GI tract.

emergency.atePlastic.banner.subtitle: Plastic is non-toxic but can cause dangerous intestinal blockage. Risk depends on the size and shape of the object. Call your vet if the piece is larger than 2cm.
emergency.atePlastic.decisionGuide.safe: Plastic piece smaller than 2cm (e.g., corner of wrapper). Monitor stool for 48 hours.
emergency.atePlastic.decisionGuide.call: Plastic piece 2-3cm OR your dog shows ANY vomiting/lethargy. X-ray may be needed.
emergency.atePlastic.decisionGuide.emerg: Plastic larger than 3cm, OR persistent vomiting, OR no bowel movement in 48 hours. Surgery likely needed.
emergency.atePlastic.science.content: Plastic is chemically inert and non-toxic to dogs — the danger is purely mechanical. The canine GI tract narrows at two critical points: the pylorus (stomach exit, ~1-2cm diameter in small dogs) and the ileocecal junction (small-to-large intestine transition). Objects wider than these passages become lodged, causing a complete or partial obstruction. Complete obstructions cause fluid accumulation, electrolyte imbalances, and intestinal necrosis within 48-72 hours. Surgical intervention is required for objects that do not pass within 24-48 hours or cause persistent vomiting (Merck Veterinary Manual, 2023).
emergency.atePlastic.toxicityData.exampl: A 2cm plastic toy ball will not pass through a medium-sized dog's pylorus. Objects >2cm require vet assessment.

emergency.ateMedication.banner.title: My Dog Ate Human Medication: What to Do Now
emergency.ateMedication.banner.subtitle: Human medications are a leading cause of pet poisoning. Even one pill of ibuprofen or acetaminophen can kill a dog. Call ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 IMMEDIATELY.
emergency.ateMedication.science.content: Dogs metabolize many drugs differently than humans. NSAIDs (ibuprofen) inhibit cyclooxygenase enzymes, reducing protective prostaglandins in the GI tract and kidneys, leading to ulceration and renal failure. Acetaminophen depletes glutathione in canine hepatocytes and converts hemoglobin to methemoglobin, impairing oxygen transport. Dogs are particularly sensitive to many ADHD medications (amphetamines) due to their effect on catecholamine release. Even "harmless" supplements like vitamin D can cause fatal hypercalcemia when ingested in large amounts (ASPCA, 2023).
emergency.ateMedication.toxicityData.min: Drug-dependent: Ibuprofen 50mg/kg, Acetaminophen 75mg/kg, single pill of some ADHD meds
emergency.ateMedication.toxicityData.exa: A single 200mg ibuprofen tablet can cause kidney failure in a 4kg dog. Five tablets (1000mg) = 250mg/kg = potentially fatal dose.

emergency.ateRodenticide.banner.subtitle: Rodenticide is one of the deadliest dog toxins. Do not wait for symptoms — anticoagulant effects are delayed 2-5 days. Call ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 and go to emergency vet NOW.
emergency.ateRodenticide.science.content: Anticoagulant rodenticides inhibit vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKOR), preventing recycling of vitamin K. This depletes active clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X), causing spontaneous hemorrhage. Second-generation anticoagulants (brodifacoum, bromadiolone) are 100x more potent than warfarin and persist in the liver for weeks. Bromethalin uncouples oxidative phosphorylation in brain cells, causing cerebral edema and increased intracranial pressure. Cholecalciferol (vitamin D3) causes hypercalcemia, leading to metastatic calcification of kidneys, heart, and blood vessels (ASPCA, 2023).

emergency.ateTobacco.science.content: Nicotine is an alkaloid that binds to nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs) in the autonomic ganglia, neuromuscular junctions, and CNS. At low doses, it stimulates receptors causing tachycardia, hypertension, and CNS excitation. At high doses, it causes receptor depolarization blockade, leading to bradycardia, respiratory paralysis, and coma. The biphasic effect (stimulation then depression) is pathognomonic. Dogs metabolize nicotine primarily via hepatic N-oxidation, with a half-life of approximately 1.5 hours. E-liquid poses extreme danger because 1mL can contain 3-24mg of nicotine absorbed rapidly through oral mucosa (ASPCA, 2023).

emergency.ateMarijuana.honestySection.co: Veterinarians are required to treat, not report, pet poisonings. Accurate information about marijuana ingestion ensures your dog receives proper care without unnecessary testing. Your honesty is protected and helps save your dog's life.
emergency.ateMarijuana.science.content: Delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) binds to CB1 cannabinoid receptors in the canine central nervous system. Dogs have a higher density of CB1 receptors in the cerebellum (responsible for coordination) and brainstem than humans, explaining their heightened sensitivity. THC is lipophilic and undergoes enterohepatic recirculation, prolonging effects. Edibles are dangerous because the GI tract absorbs THC rapidly, and the liver converts 11-hydroxy-THC, which is 5x more psychoactive. Most cases are supportive — there is no specific antidote, but IV lipid emulsion therapy can accelerate THC clearance (ASPCA, 2023).

emergency.ateXylitolGum.banner.subtitle: Xylitol triggers a massive insulin release causing life-threatening hypoglycemia and liver failure. One piece of gum can kill a small dog. Go to emergency vet NOW.
emergency.ateXylitolGum.science.content: Xylitol is a sugar alcohol (polyol) that triggers a rapid, exaggerated insulin release from canine beta cells — up to 6-7x the amount released by glucose. This is because dogs metabolize xylitol via the same pathway as glucose but with different kinetics. The resulting hypoglycemia (blood glucose <60mg/dL) causes neurological dysfunction, seizures, and death. At higher doses (>0.5g/kg), xylitol causes acute hepatic necrosis through ATP depletion and oxidative stress. The mechanism is dose-dependent and unique to dogs — cats appear to be less susceptible (ASPCA, 2023).

emergency.ateChocolate.banner.subtitle: Chocolate contains theobromine, which dogs cannot metabolize effectively. Immediate action is critical — call your vet or ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 right away.
emergency.ateChocolate.science.content: Chocolate contains theobromine and caffeine, both methylxanthines that dogs metabolize much more slowly than humans. While humans eliminate theobromine in 2-3 hours, dogs take 17.5 hours or more. This allows toxic levels to build up in their system. Theobromine affects the central nervous system, cardiovascular system, and smooth muscles. At high doses, it causes seizures, cardiac arrhythmias, and potentially death (ASPCA, 2023).

emergency.ateGrapes.science.content: The exact toxic compound in grapes and raisins remains unidentified, but tartaric acid is the leading suspect. This compound causes acute tubular necrosis in the kidneys, leading to rapid kidney failure. The toxic dose is unpredictable — some dogs develop kidney failure from just a few grapes, while others tolerate more. This variability makes any ingestion a medical emergency (ASPCA, 2023).

emergency.ateXylitol.science.content: Xylitol is a sugar alcohol that triggers a rapid, massive insulin release from the dog's pancreas. This causes blood sugar to plummet within 10-30 minutes. At higher doses, xylitol causes acute liver failure through mechanisms that are not fully understood. Unlike humans, dogs absorb xylitol rapidly and their bodies mistake it for real sugar, triggering this dangerous insulin response (ASPCA, 2023).

emergency.ateOnion.science.content: Onions contain thiosulfate compounds (n-propyl disulfide) that dogs cannot metabolize. These compounds cause oxidative damage to red blood cells, forming Heinz bodies — damaged hemoglobin that precipitates inside the cell. The spleen then destroys these damaged cells, leading to hemolytic anemia. This process takes 1-3 days, which is why symptoms are delayed (ASPCA, 2023).

emergency.ateSock.science.content: Fabric foreign bodies are particularly dangerous because they can become lodged at the pyloric sphincter (stomach exit) or in the small intestine. Once stuck, they cause a complete blockage — nothing can pass, and the intestinal wall may become necrotic (die) from pressure. This leads to perforation, peritonitis, and death without surgical intervention. Puppies and small dogs are at highest risk due to their narrower intestinal diameter (AVMA, 2023).

emergency.ateAntifreeze.banner.subtitle: Antifreeze (ethylene glycol) causes rapid kidney failure and death. As little as 1 teaspoon can kill — call your vet or ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 IMMEDIATELY.
emergency.ateAntifreeze.science.content: Ethylene glycol itself is not toxic — it is the metabolites produced by the liver that cause damage. Alcohol dehydrogenase converts ethylene glycol to glycoaldehyde, then glycolic acid, then oxalic acid. Oxalic acid binds with calcium to form calcium oxalate crystals that destroy kidney tissue. This process causes metabolic acidosis and acute kidney failure within 12-36 hours. The antidote works by blocking alcohol dehydrogenase, preventing toxic metabolite formation (ASPCA, 2023).

catEmergency.ateChocolate.science.conten: Chocolate contains theobromine and caffeine — methylxanthines that cats cannot efficiently metabolize. Cytochrome P450 enzymes in feline liver have reduced activity compared to dogs, causing prolonged theobromine half-life. This leads to cumulative effects on the CNS (seizures), cardiovascular system (arrhythmias), and smooth muscles. Cats are also obligate carnivores with less capacity to process plant-derived alkaloids. The combination of smaller body weight, slower metabolism, and greater sensitivity makes chocolate proportionally more dangerous for cats (ASPCA, 2023).

catEmergency.ateOnion.science.content: Onions (Allium cepa) contain N-propyl disulfide and S-methylcysteine sulfoxide. These compounds cause oxidative damage to hemoglobin, forming Heinz bodies (denatured hemoglobin precipitates). The spleen removes damaged cells, causing hemolytic anemia. Cats are especially vulnerable because feline hemoglobin contains more sulfhydryl groups than other species, making it more susceptible to oxidation. Additionally, cats have lower glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) activity, reducing their ability to protect red blood cells from oxidative injury. Anemia typically peaks 3-5 days post-ingestion (Merck Veterinary Manual, 2023).

catEmergency.ateGarlic.science.content: Garlic (Allium sativum) contains alliin, which converts to allicin when crushed or chewed. Allicin and its derivatives (allyl propyl disulfide, ajoene) cause oxidative denaturation of hemoglobin in feline erythrocytes. The feline hemoglobin molecule has 8-10 sulfhydryl groups (vs 2-4 in dogs), making it 2-3x more susceptible to oxidative damage. The resulting Heinz bodies are phagocytosed by splenic macrophages, causing extravascular hemolysis. Unlike onions, garlic's thiosulfates are more bioavailable in cats due to differences in hepatic metabolism (Merck Veterinary Manual, 2023).

What to do if your cat is exposed to essential oils.
catEmergency.ateEssentialOils.science.co: Cats lack UDP-glucuronosyltransferase (UGT1A6 and UGT1A9) enzymes required for phase II glucuronidation of terpenes (d-limonene, alpha-terpineol) and phenols (eugenol, thymol). These compounds accumulate in the hepatobiliary system, causing hepatotoxicity and neurotoxicity. Cats also have deficient P-glycoprotein efflux transporters at the blood-brain barrier, increasing CNS exposure. Tea tree oil (Melaleuca alternifolia) monoterpenes cause dose-dependent CNS depression, ataxia, and hypothermia. Even 10mL applied dermally can be fatal in cats (ASPCA, 2023).

catEmergency.ateFishingLine.science.cont: Linear foreign bodies (string, yarn, fishing line) are surgical emergencies in cats. The proximal end anchors — commonly under the tongue, at the pylorus, or in the stomach. Intestinal peristalsis pulls the distal end taught, causing the intestine to plicate (accordion-fold) around it. The taut line exerts pressure on the mesenteric border, causing ischemic necrosis and perforation. Multiple perforations along the intestinal tract lead to septic peritonitis. Unlike dogs, cats have a smaller intestinal diameter and are more susceptible to linear foreign body complications (AAHA, 2023).

catEmergency.ateLily.science.content: The exact toxic compound in lilies is unidentified, but it causes acute tubular necrosis in feline kidneys. Cats are uniquely susceptible — dogs and humans can eat lilies without harm. The toxin is water-soluble and present in all plant parts: petals, leaves, stems, pollen, and even vase water. Kidney damage begins within hours and progresses to complete renal failure within 24-72 hours without treatment. Early IV fluid therapy (within 18 hours) can prevent permanent damage (ASPCA, 2023).

catEmergency.ateString.article.ogDescrip: Emergency guide: What to do if your cat eats string. Linear foreign body danger and intestinal damage risk.
catEmergency.ateString.science.content: Linear foreign bodies (string, yarn, thread, tinsel) are uniquely dangerous because they anchor at one point — typically under the tongue or at the pyloric sphincter — while the rest is pulled through the intestines by normal peristalsis (intestinal contractions). This causes the intestines to bunch up ("pleat") along the string, and the taut string can saw through the intestinal wall like a wire. This leads to perforation, peritonitis, sepsis, and death without surgical intervention. Cats are especially prone due to their barbed tongues that easily catch string (AAFP, 2023).

about.title: About petsMetrics
about.intro: Built by petsMetrics Team, a pet owner and developer. petsMetrics has been providing science-based pet health tools since 2026. We believe pet owners deserve accurate, transparent calculators that don't require accounts, emails, or personal data.
about.methodologyP1: All calorie formulas are based on the AAFCO 2023 Nutrient Profiles. Dog age conversion uses the UCSD epigenetic methylation study (Wang et al., 2020). Cat age conversion follows AAHA/AAFP 2021 Feline Life Stage Guidelines. Vaccination schedules reference WSAVA 2024 Global Vaccination Guidelines. Toxicity data is verified against the ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center database and AVMA guidelines (last checked: June 2026).
about.methodologyP2: Every calculator result page cites its formula source. You can verify any of our formulas independently — search "RER 70 × weight^0.75 AAFCO" or "UCSD dog aging epigenetic clock Wang 2020" and confirm the science yourself. We don't invent formulas; we implement peer-reviewed veterinary research.
about.dataSourcesP1: Toxicity information verified against ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center database and AVMA guidelines (last checked: June 2026). Our toxic food and plant database contains 200+ items drawn from the ASPCA's publicly available toxic and non-toxic plant lists, Pet Poison Helpline data, and peer-reviewed veterinary literature. We update this database annually to reflect the latest ASPCA findings.
about.dataSourcesP2: Breed data (weight standards, life expectancy, genetic health risks) is sourced from AKC (American Kennel Club) and TICA (The International Cat Association) breed standards. EU pet travel rules are based on EU Regulation 576/2013 and individual member state national agriculture ministry publications.
